blocks.title: Honors — justify WHICH equation
blocks.markdown: There are several kinematic equations and they all look plausible. CPA plugs into the one that works. Honors chooses on purpose — and can say why the others don't apply.

## Pick the equation by what's missing

The constant-acceleration equations each leave out exactly one variable:

- $v = v_0 + at$ — no displacement $\Delta x$.
- $\Delta x = v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ — no final velocity $v$.
- $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\,\Delta x$ — no time $t$.

So the honest selection rule is: **list your knowns, identify your unknown, and pick the equation that contains your unknown and none of the variables you don't have.** You're not hunting for a formula that 'works' — you're matching the equation to the information you actually possess.

And every one of them rests on one assumption: **acceleration is constant** over the interval. If $a$ changes, none of these apply.

blocks.prompt: A probe starts at $v_0 = 200$ m/s and accelerates uniformly at $a = 12$ m/s² over a displacement of $\Delta x = 5{,}000$ m. Find its final velocity. In your work, FIRST state which kinematic equation you chose and WHY the other two don't fit this problem.
blocks.givenHint: You have v0, a, and Δx — and you are NOT given time t.
blocks.equationHint: Choose the equation that contains your unknown (v) and does NOT require the variable you're missing (t).

blocks.frame: I chose $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$ because my knowns were ___ and my unknown was ___, and the other equations failed because ___. All of these assume ___.
blocks.prompt: JUSTIFY: Explain how you decided WHICH kinematic equation to use for the probe problem — name the variable that was missing and how that ruled the others out. Then name the assumption all three equations share.
